content: Vanillin could help form wound-care materials while supplying antibacterial activity, a combination made more practical by its low-cost and abundant supply. The compound behind vanilla’s sweet aroma could become an ingredient in wound-care materials. A team from Flinders University’s Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory has found that vanillin has pronounced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties, making it a candidate for formulations designed to help wounds heal. The researchers examined vanillin through a food-to-function framework, connecting its chemistry with its biological activity and potential biomedical uses. Those possibilities include incorporating it into materials and using it to help deliver drugs. Professor Krasimir Vasilev, Professor of Biomedical Nanotechnology at Flinders University and Director of Flinders’ Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory, says, “Because vanillin’s synthetic form is abundant and cost-effective, we believe vanillin-based formulations may offer safe and multifunctional solutions for ulcer treatment and targeted drug delivery, especially of hydrophobic compounds. “Owing to its amphiphilic molecular structure, vanillin can interact with reactive oxygen species, cellular membranes, and polymeric matrices, providing a basis for its incorporation into functional formulations.” Amphiphilic molecules contain both water-attracting and water-repelling regions, while hydrophobic compounds do not dissolve readily in water. In material design, vanillin can also serve as a dynamic crosslinker, helping form reversible connections between the long molecular chains that make up polymers. It can therefore contribute to a material’s structure as well as its biological activity. Vanillin is the primary chemical component extracted from natural vanilla pods, but it can also be produced synthetically from clove oil or rice. Its widespread use in foods gives researchers a familiar starting point for exploring other applications. “Vanillin is among the most widely used flavor compounds in the global food system, valued for its sensory attributes, chemical stability, and long history of safety—and that can be transferred to other areas, such as medical uses,” says Vasilev. The researchers see practical advantages in vanillin’s availability as a low-cost small molecule suitable for good manufacturing practices. These characteristics could support industrial-scale production, consistent formulations, and reliable supply chains. The laboratory’s interest in food-derived medical materials grew partly from Vasilev’s experience of eating peppermint leaves from a drink and noticing significant relief from a sore throat. That observation prompted him to investigate whether peppermint’s biological activity could be incorporated into a durable coating through plasma technology, a field he has researched for more than two decades. In work published in the journal Small in February 2026, the Flinders team created a nanoscale coating derived from peppermint oil. The coating protects against infection, inflammation, and oxidative stress while remaining compatible with human tissue and suitable for use on medical materials. The vanillin research continues this exploration of food compounds as potential ingredients in medical technologies. “With coordinated engagement between academia, clinicians, and industry, vanillin has the potential to progress from an underutilized bioactive to a clinically deployable component of next-generation wound care and regenerative therapeutics,” says Vasilev. Reference: “Vanillin as a bioactive component in biomedical formulations for chronic wound healing and tissue regeneration” by Borislav Stoilov, Vi Khanh Truong, Christopher Delaney and Krasimir Vasilev, 2 August 2026, International Journal of Pharmaceutics . DOI: 10.1016/j.ijpharm.2026.127263 K.V. thanks NHMRC, Australia for Fellowship GNT1194466. A small ear stimulation device could offer a new way to tackle high blood pressure that stays elevated despite medication. Researchers at Queen Mary University of London have tested a device that stimulates nerves through the ear in people whose high blood pressure remained uncontrolled despite medication. The trial, published in the American Heart Association journal Hypertension , found that the treatment was safe and practical to use at home. Finding additional ways to control blood pressure matters because many people receiving treatment still exceed recommended targets. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart attack and stroke. The approach, transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), delivers electrical stimulation without an invasive procedure. It targets the autonomic nervous system, which helps regulate blood pressure through functions outside conscious control. The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, delivers gentle electrical pulses through two clips attached to the tragus, the small piece of cartilage at the front of the ear. Patients can administer the treatment themselves at home. The NIHR-funded SCRATCH-HTN trial included 63 participants whose hypertension remained uncontrolled while taking one or more blood pressure medications. They were randomly assigned to receive either active stimulation or a sham device, allowing researchers to compare outcomes between the groups. Participants used their devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks, then once weekly for another 10 weeks. They followed the schedule closely, and treatment was safe and well tolerated during the trial. Those findings establish that the approach was practical to use but do not establish that it effectively lowers blood pressure compared to sham devices. Across the full study population, active treatment did not produce a significantly greater blood pressure reduction than the sham device. However, a subgroup analysis planned before the trial found a larger reduction with active treatment among people who began with more severe hypertension. That result provides a direction for further research. Larger trials focused on specific patient groups will need to establish whether the difference holds up and identify who, if anyone, benefits. Dr. Ajay Gupta, the chief investigator, a clinical reader at Queen Mary University of London and a consultant physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said: “This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham. “As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension.” Reference: “Safety, Acceptability and Efficacy of Noninvasive Transcutaneous-Autonomic Neuromodulation in Uncontrolled Hypertension” by Ajay Gupta, David Collier, James Steckelmacher, Jane Field, George Collett, Olivier Zongo, Mital Patel, Manish Saxena, Annastazia Learoyd, Amrita Ahluwalia and Peter Sever, 28 September 2026, Hypertension . A small trial in older adults uncovered subtle gut changes and hints of mood improvement with daily blueberry powder, but no clear benefit over placebo. Inside the gut, the fiber and dark pigments in blueberries encounter a crowded community of microbes. Those ingredients could change the microbes and the substances they produce, raising the possibility that eating the fruit might influence mood. Establishing whether those microscopic changes actually ease depressive symptoms requires evidence that reaches beyond the gut. Courtney L. Millar, PhD, and her colleagues explored that possibility in a three-month pilot study of sedentary adults 65 and older with mild depressive symptoms. Participants who consumed blueberry powder daily showed a greater, more consistent reduction in symptoms than those given a placebo. The difference between the groups was not statistically significant, however, leaving the apparent benefit uncertain. “Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults,” said Millar, the study’s lead author and an assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife’s Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research. Anthocyanins are the pigments that give blueberries their rich color, while metabolites are substances produced through chemical processes, including those carried out by microbes. Participants were randomly assigned to consume either 48 grams, about 1.7 ounces, of blueberry powder each day or a matched placebo powder. The blueberry portion represented approximately two cups of fresh berries. The trial was double-blind, meaning neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them knew who was receiving which powder. Millar’s team paired questionnaires measuring depressive symptoms with laboratory analyses of stool samples collected before and after the intervention. “Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms,” said Millar, who is also an assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. Reading microbial DNA allowed the researchers to measure which species and genes were present and how abundant they were. Separate chemical analyses measured short-chain fatty acids, substances produced by gut microbes. Together, these measurements let the team examine both the microbial community and some of its chemical products. Several categories of genes associated with microbial enzymes changed significantly within the blueberry group. One involved polyamine-transporting ATPase, which the researchers describe as participating in the production of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA. Changes in the abundance of those genes do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the microbes produced more GABA or that it affected participants’ mood. Other measurements remained unchanged, including the abundance of microbial species, the metabolic pathways assessed, and the short-chain fatty acids measured in stool. The genetic findings therefore represented a narrow change within the gut microbiome, without a corresponding change in those measured chemical products. Eighteen older adults completed the study, including 10 who consumed blueberry powder daily and eight who received a placebo. Researchers observed subtle shifts in microbial genes in the blueberry group, alongside greater reductions in depressive symptoms, pointing to a possible connection between blueberry compounds, the gut microbiome, and mood. Reference: “A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms” by Courtney L. Millar, Mohit P. Chopra, Xochitl Morgan, Emily A. Green, Alex Wolfe, Kerry A. Pierce, Lidan Gao, Christopher N. Blesso, Alyssa B. Dufour, Douglas P. Kiel and Lewis A. Lipsitz, 21 August 2026, The Journal of nutrition, health and aging . DOI: 10.1016/j.jnha.2026.100958 The Berries, Bugs, and the Blues was funded by the USDAAFRINIFA grant (2023-67017-39055).
